quotes.cite: site@Benchmarking models on verifiable biological tasks with BioMysteryBench
quotes.quote: By sourcing problems derived from controllable properties of data, BioMysteryBench does not depend on humans being able to solve the problems.

In developing this eval, questions were primarily derived from raw or minimally processed DNA or RNA sequencing data since this is where many biological processing pipelines begin (WGS, scRNA-seq, methylation, ChIP-seq, metagenomics, Hi-C), and also included several questions drawn from proteomics and metabolomics.
we required each question author to submit a validation notebook demonstrating that the signal does, in fact, exist in the data (even if finding it from scratch might be difficult)
Which human organ is this cell type single-cell RNA-seq dataset derived from?
What gene was knocked out in the experimental samples compared to the control samples based on RNA-seq data?
From WGS sequences, what sample is the mother of sample X and what sample is the father?
Which of the bigWig files are from ChIP samples and which are from input controls?
Given H3K27ac ChIP-seq peaks from an unknown cell type, identify the cell type.

For each question, we tasked up to five domain experts to answer the question from scratch. Once a question was answered correctly by at least one human, we considered it human-solvable. BioMysteryBench contained 76 such tasks.
Accuracy averaged over 5 trials per 76 human-solvable problems. Error bars computed by bootstrap sampling within problems.
After QC’ing with benchmarkers and additional experts, we removed 4 questions that were due to (1), leaving 23 human-difficult questions.
Accuracy over the set of problems humans were not able to solve, averaged across 5 episodes per problem.
Interestingly, Claude Sonnet 4.6 and more capable models were able to solve significant fractions of human-difficult problems, with Claude Mythos Preview topping out at a 30% solve rate.

Like many of the benchmarks we've discussed, BioMysteryBench has its own limitation: for tasks that neither humans nor models have solved, we can never be fully certain whether they're impossible or just extraordinarily difficult.
The validation notebooks help ensure the signal is there and the data is well-formed, but they do not guarantee a model or human can find the answer from scratch.

Models run with the Terminus 2 agent harness inside sandboxes configured for bioinformatics work.
Tasks were limited to 200 agent turns and four hours of wall-clock execution.
Each displayed score is the mean of three independent full-benchmark runs
Each task is evaluated from the agent’s submitted answer by a separately configured judge (we use openai/gpt-5.6-terra
Task scores are binary: a fully accepted answer scores 1, while judge-rejected answers and model/provider failures or refusals score 0.
Up to five domain experts attempted each problem, and the tasks solved by at least one expert were labeled human-solvable
Tasks refused by biology content filters are counted as task failures for the purposes of evaluation.
BioMysteryBench is a benchmark developed by Anthropic to measure agentic biological analysis performance.
Tasks cover areas including sequencing, expression analysis, variant calling, epigenomics, metagenomics, proteomics, and metabolomics.
We find that models overwhelmingly choose to give confidently wrong answers instead of expressing uncertainty.
Kimi K3 is also prone to confidently wrong answers.
We analyze failure modes using an openai/gpt-5.6-terra judge that reads only the final message from each scored-incorrect trajectory.
